listening.title: Giant whales move into Greenland waters as ice disappears
listening.topic: Climate change is melting Arctic sea ice in East Greenland, allowing humpback, fin, and minke whales to access previously ice-locked coastal waters for the first time in recorded history.
listening.topic_zh: 氣候變遷正在融化東格陵蘭的北極海冰，使座頭鯨、長鬚鯨和小鬚鯨首次進入以往被冰封鎖的沿岸水域覓食。
listening.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to 6 Minute English. Today we're exploring one of the most dramatic examples of how climate change is reshaping the natural world — and it involves some of the biggest creatures on the planet. For decades, the icy coastal waters of East Greenland were simply off-limits to large whales. The sea ice acted as a physical barrier, preventing humpback, fin, and minke whales from accessing the rich feeding grounds along the shore. But all of that is changing. As global temperatures rise, that sea ice is disappearing, and scientists have documented something quite remarkable: giant whales are moving in. Researchers conducting ship-based surveys didn't spot a single humpback whale in the region until 2006. Just one year later, seven were recorded. Fast-forward to 2024, and there were 150 sightings in that same area. Scientists are calling this a major ecological regime shift — a fundamental change in the way the ocean ecosystem functions. To understand the scale of the transformation, researchers combined aerial surveys, satellite tracking of 15 tagged whales, and even testimony from local Inuit hunters. Together, these sources painted a vivid picture of thousands of whales converging on Greenland's coastal seas every summer to feed in what scientists describe as seasonal Arctic feeding frenzies. An estimated 4,000 humpbacks, 6,000 fin whales, and 6,000 minke whales visited the Greenland Sea in 2024 alone. It's an astonishing shift — but one that raises serious questions about what it means for the broader Arctic ecosystem and for the Indigenous communities who have long depended on these waters.

vocabulary.definition: A fundamental, large-scale reorganisation of an ecosystem in which the dominant species, food webs, or environmental conditions change dramatically and often irreversibly.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 生態系統的重大轉變，指主要物種、食物鏈或環境條件發生根本性且通常不可逆的重組。
vocabulary.example: The arrival of thousands of whales in previously ice-covered waters represents a profound ecological regime shift in the Arctic.

vocabulary.definition: Impossible or very difficult to reach or enter, often because of a physical barrier.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 難以進入或抵達的，通常因為有物理障礙。
vocabulary.example: The coastal feeding grounds were inaccessible to large whales for centuries because of the thick sea ice.

vocabulary.definition: A group of large marine mammals that filter food from the water using plates of baleen (whalebone) instead of teeth; includes humpback, fin, and minke whales.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 鬚鯨類，一群用鯨鬚過濾食物的大型海洋哺乳動物，包括座頭鯨、長鬚鯨和小鬚鯨。
vocabulary.example: Baleen whales rely on dense concentrations of krill and small fish, which are now more abundant in East Greenland's ice-free waters.

vocabulary.definition: Describing an animal that has been fitted with an electronic tracking device that transmits location data to satellites, enabling researchers to monitor its movements remotely.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 裝有衛星追蹤裝置的（動物），可讓研究人員遠端監測其行蹤。
vocabulary.example: Data from fifteen satellite-tagged whales helped scientists map the seasonal migration routes into Greenland's coastal waters.

vocabulary.definition: A period of intense, highly concentrated feeding activity by a large number of animals in one area, often triggered by an abundance of food.
vocabulary.definition_zh: 覓食狂潮，指大量動物在同一區域密集、激烈進食的時期，通常因食物豐富而引發。
vocabulary.example: Scientists described the summer gatherings of whales off East Greenland as seasonal Arctic feeding frenzies.

questions.q: According to the passage, when was the first humpback whale sighting recorded during ship-based surveys in East Greenland?
questions.explanation: The transcript states that ship-based surveys did not record a single humpback whale sighting in East Greenland until 2006, making B the correct answer. 2007 was when seven humpbacks were first seen, not the first sighting year.

questions.q: Which combination of data sources did researchers use to build their picture of whale activity in East Greenland?
options: A: Underwater microphones, drone footage, and fishermen's logs
B: Aerial surveys, satellite tracking, and Inuit hunters' testimony
C: Ship surveys, ocean temperature sensors, and historical records
D: Satellite imagery, submarine observations, and academic journals
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that researchers combined aerial surveys, tracks of 15 satellite-tagged whales, and testimony from Inuit hunters to build their comprehensive picture of the ecological shift.

questions.q: What does the term 'ecological regime shift' refer to in the context of this episode?
options: A: A government policy change affecting marine conservation zones
B: A temporary seasonal fluctuation in whale migration patterns
C: A fundamental reorganisation of the ocean ecosystem driven by environmental change
D: A new international agreement on Arctic wildlife protection
questions.explanation: The episode uses 'ecological regime shift' to describe the fundamental, large-scale change in how the East Greenland ocean ecosystem functions — specifically the replacement of an ice-dominated environment with whale-rich open waters — not a policy, temporary fluctuation, or agreement.

reading.title: Arctic Marine Ecosystems in Transition: Whales and the Retreat of Greenland Sea Ice
reading.passage:
The accelerating retreat of sea ice along the coast of East Greenland represents one of the most visually striking and ecologically consequential manifestations of anthropogenic climate change in the Arctic. For millennia, perennial sea ice acted as an impenetrable barrier along this coastline, preventing large cetaceans from exploiting the nutrient-rich coastal shelf. However, as ocean surface temperatures have risen in response to increasing atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, this barrier has progressively dissolved, triggering a cascade of biological changes that scientists characterise as a major ecological regime shift.

Longitudinal ship-based surveys conducted by marine biologists provide compelling quantitative evidence of the transformation. Not a single humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) was recorded in the region during such surveys prior to 2006. By 2007, seven individuals had been observed, and by the summer of 2024 the figure had risen dramatically to 150 sightings. To establish a more complete spatial picture, researchers conducted systematic aerial surveys of baleen whales — encompassing fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), minke whales (Balaenoptera acutorostrata), and humpbacks — during the summers of 2015 and 2024. These surveys were supplemented by telemetric data obtained from 15 satellite-tagged individuals and by qualitative accounts provided by Indigenous Inuit hunters with generational knowledge of the region's waters.

The aggregate findings are striking. An estimated 4,000 humpback whales, 6,000 fin whales, and 6,000 minke whales utilised the Greenland Sea during the summer of 2024, congregating in what researchers describe as seasonal feeding frenzies. These gatherings are made possible by the proliferation of krill and small pelagic fish in newly ice-free waters. While the influx of apex marine predators may enhance certain aspects of ecosystem productivity through nutrient cycling, ecologists caution that such rapid faunal changes also carry risks. The long-term consequences for zooplankton populations, benthic communities, and the traditional subsistence practices of Inuit peoples remain subjects of active scientific and ethical debate.

questions.statement: Ship-based surveys recorded humpback whales in East Greenland waters every year from 2000 onwards.
questions.explanation: The passage states that no humpback whale was recorded during ship-based surveys prior to 2006, meaning they were absent from recorded surveys in the early 2000s, not present every year from 2000.

questions.statement: Researchers used both aerial surveys and satellite tracking to study whale movements in East Greenland.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly confirms that researchers conducted systematic aerial surveys and supplemented these with telemetric data from 15 satellite-tagged whales, confirming both methods were used.

questions.statement: Scientists have conclusively determined that the arrival of whales will benefit the Inuit communities of East Greenland.
questions.explanation: The passage states that consequences for Inuit peoples' traditional subsistence practices remain subjects of active debate. No conclusive determination — positive or negative — regarding benefit to Inuit communities is presented in the text.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest is the primary reason large whales were historically absent from East Greenland's coastal waters?
options: A: Overhunting by Inuit communities had reduced whale populations to near zero
B: A lack of sufficient food sources such as krill in the region
C: Perennial sea ice formed an impenetrable physical barrier to whale access
D: International conservation laws prohibited whaling in the area
questions.explanation: The passage directly states that 'perennial sea ice acted as an impenetrable barrier along this coastline, preventing large cetaceans from exploiting the nutrient-rich coastal shelf.' Overhunting, lack of food, and conservation laws are not cited as reasons for historical absence.

speaking.topic: Describe a significant environmental change you have learned about
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一個你曾了解過的重大環境變化

part2.cue_card:
Describe a significant environmental change you have learned about.

You should say:
• what the environmental change is and where it is happening
• how you found out about it
• what effects this change is having on wildlife or people

And explain how this change made you think differently about environmental issues.
band_tips: Use precise scientific and environmental vocabulary naturally, such as 'ecological regime shift', 'biodiversity', 'cascading consequences', and 'anthropogenic factors', to demonstrate lexical sophistication without sounding scripted.

Structure your response clearly: briefly introduce the change, describe its causes using the passive voice and complex sentence structures, then discuss its consequences at multiple levels — wildlife, ecosystem, and human communities — before reflecting on your own perspective shift.

Aim for fluency and cohesion by using discourse markers such as 'what is particularly striking is that...', 'as a consequence of this', and 'it was only when I read about this that I realised...' to link ideas smoothly and show examiner-level spoken grammar range.

part3.q: To what extent do you think human activity is responsible for changes in Arctic ecosystems?
part3.q_zh: 你認為人類活動在多大程度上應為北極生態系統的變化負責？
key_points: The scientific consensus strongly attributes Arctic warming to anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, with the Arctic warming at roughly four times the global average rate — candidates can cite this to demonstrate awareness of scale.

It is worth distinguishing between direct impacts such as shipping, pollution, and hunting, and indirect impacts such as climate change caused by industrial emissions in distant regions, as this nuance shows critical thinking.

Candidates can acknowledge that natural climate variability exists but argue that the speed and scale of current changes are unprecedented in the geological record and point overwhelmingly to human causation.

part3.q: How might the arrival of large whales in new Arctic areas affect the local communities who have traditionally lived there?
part3.q_zh: 大型鯨魚進入北極新區域，可能會如何影響當地傳統社區的生活？
key_points: Indigenous Inuit communities have practised subsistence hunting and fishing for generations; a sudden influx of large whale predators may alter local fish and krill populations that these communities depend on for food security.
There could be economic opportunities arising from whale-watching ecotourism, but these benefits may be unevenly distributed and could conflict with traditional cultural values and ways of life.

The involvement of Inuit hunters as knowledge holders in the scientific study illustrates a positive model of collaboration, and candidates could argue for greater Indigenous participation in environmental decision-making going forward.

part3.q: Do you think the media focuses too much on dramatic wildlife stories and not enough on the underlying causes of climate change?
part3.q_zh: 你認為媒體是否過度關注戲劇性的野生動物故事，而忽略了氣候變遷的根本原因？
key_points: Attention-grabbing stories about whales or polar bears can serve as accessible entry points that raise public awareness and emotional engagement with abstract issues like greenhouse gas emissions and global temperature rise.

However, critics argue that focusing on spectacular natural phenomena risks 'spectacularising' climate change, leading audiences to see it as a distant natural wonder rather than an urgent crisis requiring political and behavioural action.

High-quality journalism should ideally connect compelling wildlife narratives to systemic causes, policy failures, and individual responsibilities, using storytelling as a bridge rather than an endpoint.

part3.q: What responsibilities do governments and international organisations have in protecting marine ecosystems like those in the Arctic?
part3.q_zh: 各國政府和國際組織在保護北極等海洋生態系統方面有哪些責任？
key_points: Governments have a duty to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under international frameworks such as the Paris Agreement, as reducing warming is the only way to prevent further irreversible loss of Arctic sea ice and the ecosystems it supports.

International organisations like the International Whaling Commission and the Arctic Council play roles in coordinating cross-border conservation efforts, as marine ecosystems and migratory species do not respect national boundaries.

There is a compelling argument for the precautionary principle — that in the absence of complete scientific certainty, governments should err on the side of environmental protection, particularly for fragile and rapidly changing ecosystems like the Arctic.

writing.task2_question: Climate change is causing significant and irreversible changes to natural ecosystems around the world. Some people argue that governments should prioritise economic development over environmental protection, while others believe that protecting ecosystems must take precedence. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 氣候變遷正對全球自然生態系統造成重大且不可逆的改變。有些人認為政府應將經濟發展置於環境保護之上，而另一些人則認為保護生態系統應優先考慮。討論兩種觀點並給出你自己的意見。

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the introduction or when presenting a well-established fact or scientific consensus to establish credibility before developing your argument.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於引言或陳述廣為接受的事實或科學共識時，在展開論點前建立可信度。
useful_phrases.example: It is widely acknowledged that the retreat of Arctic sea ice is accelerating at an unprecedented rate, with profound consequences for marine biodiversity.

useful_phrases.phrase: While it is true that... , it must be acknowledged that...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to concede a point from the opposing view before pivoting to your own stronger counterargument, demonstrating balanced and sophisticated reasoning.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於承認對方觀點後，轉而提出自己更有力的反駁論點，展現平衡且成熟的推理能力。
useful_phrases.example: While it is true that economic growth can lift millions out of poverty, it must be acknowledged that the collapse of natural ecosystems would ultimately undermine the very foundations of long-term prosperity.

useful_phrases.phrase: The consequences of... extend far beyond...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when you want to broaden the scope of an argument and show that an issue has wider ramifications than might initially be apparent.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 當你想擴大論點範疇，說明某議題的影響遠超過表面所見時使用。
useful_phrases.example: The consequences of losing Arctic biodiversity extend far beyond the region itself, disrupting global ocean circulation patterns and carbon storage systems.

useful_phrases.phrase: A compelling case can be made for...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to introduce your own opinion or a strongly supported position in a measured, academic tone that avoids sounding overly assertive or informal.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於以學術、適度的語氣介紹自己的觀點或有力的立場，避免語氣過於強硬或非正式。
useful_phrases.example: A compelling case can be made for integrating environmental protection targets directly into national economic planning frameworks rather than treating them as competing priorities.

useful_phrases.phrase: In the long run, failure to address... will inevitably result in...
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the conclusion or a body paragraph to emphasise long-term consequences and reinforce the urgency of taking action on a particular issue.
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於結論或段落中強調長期後果，並強化在特定議題上採取行動的迫切性。
useful_phrases.example: In the long run, failure to address the root causes of marine ecosystem degradation will inevitably result in economic losses that dwarf the short-term costs of protective regulation.

outline.intro: Begin by contextualising the debate with reference to a concrete example — such as the dramatic ecological changes observed in Arctic marine environments — to immediately engage the reader. Paraphrase the question, briefly acknowledge the tension between economic and environmental imperatives, and clearly state that while economic concerns are valid, environmental protection must ultimately take precedence for long-term human welfare.
outline.body1: Present the case for prioritising economic development: argue that rapid industrialisation has lifted billions from poverty, that emerging economies have a legitimate claim to the same development pathways used by wealthy nations, and that technological innovation driven by economic growth may itself produce environmental solutions. Use cautious language to represent this view fairly before signalling a transition.
outline.body2: Present and develop the case for environmental prioritisation as the stronger position: argue that ecosystems provide irreplaceable services — clean water, climate regulation, food security — whose monetary value far exceeds short-term industrial gains; cite examples such as the collapse of fisheries or the cascading consequences of Arctic biodiversity loss to show that environmental degradation ultimately destroys economic foundations; and argue that sustainable development frameworks prove the two goals need not be mutually exclusive.
outline.conclusion: Restate your opinion clearly and concisely without introducing new arguments. Emphasise that governments must adopt a long-term perspective, integrating environmental safeguards into economic policy rather than treating them as opposing forces. End with a forward-looking statement about the consequences of inaction for future generations.
